title: Building a Distributed Log
description: Understand the core architecture of Kafka — topics, partitions, producer acknowledgments, consumer groups, ISR, and exactly-once semantics.

segments.text: If I asked you to design a system that handles millions of events per second with guaranteed ordering and durability, where would you start? Let's build Kafka from first principles.
At its heart, Kafka is an append-only log. Producers write messages to the end. Consumers read from any position. Messages are immutable once written. This simple abstraction is incredibly powerful.

A topic is a named feed of messages. But one log can't handle millions of writes per second. So we split each topic into partitions. Each partition is an independent, ordered log stored on a different broker.

When a producer sends a message, a partition key determines which partition receives it. Messages with the same key always go to the same partition. This guarantees ordering per key — critical for things like user event streams.

Producer acknowledgments control durability. Acks equals zero: fire and forget, fastest but data may be lost. Acks equals one: leader confirms, good balance. Acks equals all: every replica confirms. Slowest, but no data loss.
Think about this trade-off carefully. You're building a payment processing system. Which ack level would you choose, and why?
segments.thought_prompt: For payment events, would you accept any data loss? What ack level makes sense?

segments.text: Each partition is replicated across multiple brokers. One replica is the leader, others are followers. The In-Sync Replica set, or ISR, tracks which followers are caught up. If the leader dies, an ISR member takes over instantly.

Consumer groups enable parallel processing. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in a group. Add more consumers to scale out — but never more consumers than partitions, or some will sit idle.

Each consumer tracks its position using an offset — the index of the last message it processed. Offsets are committed to Kafka itself. If a consumer crashes, its replacement resumes from the last committed offset.
Here's the hardest problem. A consumer reads a message, processes it, but crashes before committing the offset. When it restarts, it processes the same message again.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you guarantee exactly-once processing if consumers can crash at any point?

segments.text: Exactly-once semantics require idempotent producers, which tag each message with a sequence number, and transactional writes that atomically commit the message processing and offset update together. It's complex, but it works.

So that's Kafka's architecture. An append-only log, partitioned for parallelism, replicated for durability, with consumer groups for scaling reads. The elegance is in the simplicity of the log abstraction powering all of it.
